title: Precepts 1
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes that the 16 Bodhisattva precepts are not just rules to follow, but rather a way of life that cultivates compassion, kindness, and wisdom. By embracing these precepts with diligence and seriousness, we can develop a sense of righteousness that motivates us to act with compassion and wisdom in our daily lives. Ultimately, the precepts guide us towards living in the present moment, letting go of attachments and ego, and connecting with something greater than ourselves through every action we take.

sentences.text: Well, I'm feeling a little overwhelmed this morning because some time ago I casually said I would speak about the precepts for the sesshin that is so far away it will never come.
But now here it is, and I'm thinking to myself, three short dharma talks on the sixteen bodhisattva precepts.
Now that I'm facing this, I see what an enormous assignment it is, and I have a little regret that I foolishly agreed to it to begin with.

This morning, during zazen, a thought crossed my mind about how deep and wide these precepts are, and how much has been thought and spoken and taught about them over the generations, and how little of that teaching I am aware of and even dreamed about.
So how am I going to say anything useful at all in three short talks about the precepts?
It's really an awesome and daunting assignment.
I'm saying this as a warning in advance that you shouldn't expect too much, and that for sure I will just be scratching the surface, I know, before even beginning.
But as is always the case in life, one cheerfully goes on and does the best one can under the circumstances, so that's what I'm going to do.
You won't hear me complain anymore.
I just thought I'd say that at the beginning because I was really feeling it.
Last night, in our period of zazen, I asked all of you to do your best to sit diligently and with a strong seriousness of purpose and with heart, and I hope that you will do this.
This is a precious few days; it's difficult to find a few days like this to come together to sit, so please use your time well.
Take care of your posture.
Sit up straight, and stretch up toward the sky.

Be with your breathing and your belly, and concentrate yourself with all your heart and all your soul and all your mind on the feeling of being sitting and being breathing and nothing else, intensely present with that.
As I said also last night, our practice really isn't about doing it right, not doing it wrong, or even about some technique of being alert and aware.
Rather, it's really about embracing and being embraced by our life, completely entering our life, whatever it is, completely immersing ourselves, occupying fully our lives.
Maybe these days in sitting in the way that I'm urging you to sit, you can get a feeling for what I mean by these words.

And when you do that, when you really embrace your life, are embraced by it, fully occupy the life that you have been given, it's very clear that your life isn't just your life, the small life that we all think we have.
I was born on such and such a day, in such and such a place.
I lived here and there.
I was educated here and there.
I did this.
I did that.
I married.
I didn't marry, whatever it is, all of that.
This life doesn't really cover the life that you are really living when you are really living your life.
And if you will sit with full intensity, intimately being body and mind, you will come to recognize what your life actually is: that it is, just is.
And being just is, really it's ungraspable.
It's all mixed up with the timelessness of time and the spacelessness of space and with the everywhere effective love that is the force that allows life to be life.

So this is why in a way it's quite natural and a good thing to talk about precepts during sesshin because it's only through immersion in our zazen practice that we can really appreciate the essence of the meaning of the sixteen great bodhisattva precepts.
And they are called bodhisattva precepts.
And as then practitioners, our way is the way of the bodhisattva.
All of us are bodhisattvas in process, bodhisattvas in training.
Many times I'm sure you've heard me speak about what bodhisattvas are.

The word literally means enlightening beings, beings who work for enlightenment enthusiastically, stupidly, innocently, naively, pushing forward to enlighten all sentient beings, no matter how long it takes or what the cost or the difficulty, cheerfully going forward with this impossible project like the Man of La Mancha, the impossible dream of enlightenment for all sentient beings in the absolutely perfect world.
This is the lunatic bodhisattva way.

Bodhisattvas, as you also, no doubt know, are inspired by this sudden flash of inspiration that bursts into their lives somewhere from the distant past, which is called in Buddhism bodhicitta, this flashing, sudden thought of awakening, this opening of the door of enthusiasm and effort.
With bodhicitta lighting up our lives, we make effort every day to be in solidarity with and communion with all sentient beings.
And that's how we understand, as bodhisattvas, all of our activity.
Everything is in communion with and in solidarity with all sentient beings, even brushing our teeth and going to the toilet.
We're going to the toilet on behalf of everyone.
We're brushing our teeth to clean all the teeth that there ever were.
That's the feeling and the understanding and the vision of a bodhisattva's way of activity.
No, they say in the tradition that there's three kinds of bodhisattvas: the kings, the boatmen, and the shepherds.
Kings are the bodhisattvas who work for enlightenment so that after they get enlightened, they can help all sentient beings.
Those are the king bodhisattvas.

The boat people bodhisattvas are the ones who get all the sentient beings in a boat and together with them ferry across to the other side, ferry across the ocean of suffering and pain to the other side.
And the shepherd bodhisattvas are the ones who, like shepherds, make sure that all the flock is safe and gets over to safety first and then they go last.
So that's the kind of bodhisattvas that we are.
That's the practice that we do: the shepherd bodhisattva practice.
And that is the spirit, the spirit of the shepherd, of guiding others across and then going last.
That is the main spirit of the sixteen bodhisattva precepts: the spirit of humility and of loving kindness for others.
Our particular tradition of Soto Zen is actually very esoteric.
I'm sorry to say it's a little bit; it really is that way.
Which is an odd thing because at the same time that it's esoteric, it's also very ordinary.
So it's a funny paradox, you know, something very practical and down to earth and ordinary at the same time, very essentially esoteric.
On the one hand, the sixteen bodhisattva precepts are simply the way to live: ordinary, common sense, code of conduct.
Just the way we take care of ourselves and of each other on a daily basis.
It's just common sense.
Any ordinary person would understand not to lie, not to steal, not to speak unkindly of others, try to keep the mind and the heart clear.
This is no mystery; it's just common sense.
Everybody knows about this, and this is the sixteen bodhisattva precepts: just ordinary human common sense to be kind to others, to live a life that's sane and peaceful.
But also in Soto Zen the sixteen bodhisattva precepts are understood simultaneously as the deepest mystery of the Buddhist heart.
The sixteen bodhisattva precepts are understood as the ultimate and ineffable truth.

In our tradition, the most profound of all esoteric rituals is the Dharma transmission ceremony, which occurs after many, many years of study and training in secret, in private, in the abbot's room, literally in the middle of the night.
It's always held in the middle of the night in secret while everybody's sleeping.
And in that ceremony what is transmitted, the secret ineffable essence that's transmitted, is the sixteen bodhisattva precepts.
In a beautiful ritual these precepts are transmitted just as they're transmitted in all other Soto Zen rituals.

And at that time the disciple learns the secret truth, which I will now tell you because it's not really that secret anyway, that the sixteen bodhisattva precepts are just like we have, you know, blood that runs in our veins to make us live.
That the blood that runs through the veins of the Buddhas and ancestors is the life blood of the sixteen bodhisattva precepts.
This is the essence that flows through the literal body of these Buddhas and is passed down one to another, down to the present.
So the precepts are the actual blood lineage of the Buddhas, it says in our tradition; they're vital life blood.
The precepts transcend space and time and are beyond all our capacity to understand them.
And that we spend a lifetime, maybe even many lifetimes, and still we're unable to exhaust their wonderful meaning.
And yet, as I say, the mystery is that at the same time they're just manifested in ordinary daily conduct, in the ordinary acts of loving kindness that light up our lives every day.
So that's the wonderful mystery of our tradition.
I have a commentary that was written in the eighteenth century in the sixteen bodhisattva precepts by Banjin Dothan.

And he says at the very beginning, just to give you a flavor for how these things are understood in our tradition, the great precepts of all Buddhas have been protected and maintained by all Buddhas and have been mutually entrusted from Buddha to Buddha, mutually transmitted from ancestor to ancestor.
Receiving the precepts goes beyond the three times past, present, teacher.
Confirming the precepts penetrates throughout past and present.
Our great teacher, Shakyamuni Buddha, conferred them upon Mahakasyapa, Mahakasyapa conferred them upon Ananda, and so on.
In this way the precepts have been legitimately conferred up to the present abode as the ninety-two nd generation successor.
So, wow.

So, the sixteen bodhisattva precepts, what I'm trying to say, the sixteen bodhisattva precepts are not little rules to live by.
I mean, they are in a way, but they're more than that.
They really are the essence of the practice.
Again, as I said last night, our practice is not about meditation.
Really, it's not really about meditation.
It's not about insight.
It's really about conduct: how we live.
That's the important thing.
How do we live?
How do we conduct ourselves on a moment-by-moment basis through each of the days of our lives?
How do we conduct ourselves in relation to our own precious life and in relation to the lives of those around us?
That's really the essence of our practice.
There's an old saying in Zen, pick up one dust, one speck of dust, and the whole world comes with it.
And that's how we approach our conduct.
Each of our acts, even brushing our teeth, even going to the toilet, has immense dimensions and immense repercussions.
So we approach all the moments of our lives with tremendous respect and reverence, doing our best.
And we know that in the great scope of things, how could we really know what to do?
How could we ever really know the effects of our actions?
But we also feel, through our sitting practice, day by day, retreat by retreat, over time, for those of you who are new to the practice, I'm sorry to say it's not a short-term arrangement.
I wish it were.
I wish I could say, weekend retreat, after that, no problem, everything is okay.
But it isn't like that.
Life isn't like that.
Listen, if there was something that were like that other than our practice, I would be there before you.
And I'm always ready to find such a thing.
And I'm always ready to find such a thing.
But so far, I haven't seen anything like that.
I haven't seen any other way than effort over time.

When you do make effort over time, though, you find, little by little, somehow, that there's a real rock-solid sense of confidence in our life as Buddha's life, or in Buddha's life welling up through our life.
So even though we don't exactly know what to do, or we don't exactly know the consequences of our actions, we have confidence.
And we do know, for sure, somehow, through, as I say, effort over time in our sitting practice, that good actions lead to good results, and bad actions will bring bad results.

And that we have a firm and clear, pretty much unshakable confidence in this, and commitment to doing good and letting go as much as we possibly can of bad actions of body, speech, and mind that we might naturally be inspired to do.
We know to let go of them because we know that they will bring suffering.
And in this process, the precepts are a good guide and also a good inspiration.
It's very difficult to know, and the older you get and the more you do and see in your lifetime, the clearer it is, how hard it is to really know what's good and what's bad.
When you're young, you know exactly what's good and bad.
But when you get older, it's more difficult to know.

But we have a commitment to trying our best according to our understanding of the present moment, as best we understand now, to do what we can, that we understand to be the good and to trust that things will work out as they need to.
Sometimes, in the short run, something that seemed very good turns out to be an utter disaster.
Sometimes something that seemed utterly disastrous and wrong turns out to be good somehow.
This is very good to remember if you've got politics.
In other words, we know that we will certainly break precepts.
We won't be able to do good all the time, even though we intend to.
We will break them in small ways and maybe in big ways.
But our commitment is to recognize that when it's so, to let go of our sense of righteousness about our conduct, and to try to do better, to try to learn, to expand our understanding for next time.
So there's never any need in working with the precepts to feel guilty or worried or uptight, upset.
Just each moment we're facing our best understanding.
What do we think is the best way to conduct ourselves?
Because we know how difficult it is to know what's good or bad and to really live this life of the bodhisattva precepts.
Naturally, we're tolerant, tolerant of ourselves and especially tolerant of others.
The sixteen bodhisattva precepts are not fundamental rules.
They're not something objective outside of us.
They're simply some human words and concepts to describe the actual shape of Buddha's mind, which is formless.
So we don't really ever try to look at somebody else and see if they're breaking any precepts or not.

It makes no sense.
Not only is it not a good idea, it just doesn't make any sense.
It's unthinkably ridiculous to think, now let's see, is that person breaking precepts or not?
It makes no sense.
It's impossible.
Only sometimes we can feel within ourselves whether we feel that we're breaking precepts, that we can't look at someone else and say such a thing.
So there's no condemning others ever, and there's no condemning oneself.
Sometimes maybe it's necessary to be strict with yourself, sometimes more difficult, perhaps, to be strict with others.

You do it because you know that strictness in a particular instance is required.

So the strictness is motivated by loving-kindness, not by righteousness.
There isn't any sense of righteousness in our understanding of the sixteen precepts.

Not seeing the real danger.
So we have to be a child, but also our own mother to help ourselves in that way, and our parents if we can.

And the last point is that to recognize and appreciate that there are three, they always say in relation to these precepts, that there are three levels of understanding, three different approaches to the precepts that have to be appreciated for each precept.
There are these three levels of understanding.
The first level is called the literal level.
The surface or common sense, regular, ordinary level of understanding the precept.
For instance, the precept, the first of the ten great precepts, don't kill means basically don't kill.
Don't kill anything.
Don't kill a bug.
Don't kill anything.
That means not only in the literal sense, take the life, but also in the psychological sense.
Don't diminish something.
Don't take away something's confidence.
Be harmless.
Have a spirit to nurture life instead of killing life.
So that's pretty clear.
Not always easy, but clear.
So that's the literal level.
The second of the three levels is called the compassion level.
On this level we recognize that the network of causality in this world is wide and subtle.
Nothing is linear.
Nothing is one dimensional.
So sometimes not to kill one thing is to kill something else.
Sometimes there's no way.
Actually more often than one thinks to avoid breaking the precept this way, we break the precept that way, that we're stuck.

There's no way that we can be pure.
For instance, we all have to eat in order to live.

So, since the purpose of these rules, as with the purpose of the sixteen Bodhisattva precepts, is to perfectly manifest kindness and to be unkind in order to uphold the rules would really be stupid and it would be much better to violate the rules in the spirit of kindness, to be kind to one another than it would be to have perfect conduct in the zendo with the spirit of unkindness.
So, we always say it doesn't matter how you do it as long as your spirit is good and we allow people to break any of the rules that are necessary out of kindness.
So, that's the second level.
Compassion, the breaking of peace, all in kindness or for the purpose of kindness.
The third level is called the ultimate level.

This understanding is the meaning of maintaining Buddha's precepts.
Besides this, do not expect any other result.

In plain English it means in this relationship, say the first precept here, that when you really get down to it, as close and as intimate as a human being can, you see that life and death are truly indivisible.

So then, on the ultimate level, we are following the precepts without any sense of constraint, without any sense of following any precepts.
We're just easily, joyfully living our life as Buddha's life, unimpeded with kindness, well enough, always.
Now, it's unfortunate that we have this word three levels, or three whatever, because it sounds like three different things.

It sounds that way.
The ultimate level is the ultimate level.
It's more important.
Bigger and better than the other ones.

Terribly dangerous.
There are three levels.
It's just a way of talking, a way of appreciating one level.
The literal level is the ultimate level.
We just have to have different ways of talking about it.
The only way the ultimate level could ever manifest in this world that we live in is in the literal level, is in the everyday, ordinary level.
There isn't some other ultimate place over there where we're going to go.
They already checked out the stars, and that looked very far away, and they didn't find any since then.
Because it's only here, it's there too.
But it's not only far away.
The ultimate level, in other words, in these terms that I've been using, only comes up on the literal level.
There's no other way that it comes up.
And if you think that the ultimate level is something over and above and beyond the literal level, as sometimes people do, this doesn't mean that you're seeing the ultimate level.
This means you're stuck in your head.
You're stuck in concepts.
You're stuck in fancy ideas.
Which, after all, are only associated with the body.
There's no body, you've got no more ideas.
So, don't mistake this, please.
It's a very, very important point.
So, we never go beyond.
There are no advanced students here.
No one ever goes beyond the simple daily acts.
No one ever goes beyond the literal level of non-stealing, non-killing, non-intoxication, and so on and so on.
We're always paying attention lovingly to all the moments of our lives, doing the best we can.
So, it's not that the ultimate level is beyond the literal level, it simply helps us to see this way of talking, helps us to see the depth involved in the literal, everyday moments of our lives.
That each moment of our conduct cuts through this world into the endless realms beyond.
So, that's a little background.

I'm going to start talking about the sixteen Bodhisattva precepts, which I will not start today, but tomorrow, unless I think of many more background things I must say before getting to the first one.
